explanation.title: Spanish Register & Formality: Speaking Appropriately in Different Contexts

sections.subtitle: Tú vs Usted: Informal vs Formal You
sections.content:
👤 TWO WAYS TO SAY YOU (singular)

📍 TÚ (informal):
Friends, family, children, peers, casual situations

→ Tú hablas español (You speak Spanish - informal)
→ Conjugates with second person singular forms

📍 USTED (formal):
Strangers, elders, authority, professional contexts, showing respect

→ Usted habla español (You speak Spanish - formal)
→ Conjugates with THIRD PERSON singular (like él/ella)

⚠️ CRITICAL:
→ Tú tienes (you have - informal)
→ Usted tiene (you have - formal, third person!)

✅ WHEN TO USE TÚ:
• Friends, classmates, siblings
• Children
• People your age in casual settings
• After someone suggests 'Háblame de tú'

✅ WHEN TO USE USTED:
• Elderly people
• Professors, doctors, bosses
• Police officers
• In stores/restaurants initially
• Meeting someone first time (especially if older/professional)

🌍 REGIONAL VARIATION:
• Latin America tends to use usted more than Spain
• Spain: tú common even with strangers in informal contexts
• Some regions use VOS instead of tú

🔄 SWITCHING:
'Podemos tutearnos' (We can use tú)
Once established, maintain consistency

💡 When in doubt: start formal (usted), wait for cues to switch to tú

sections.subtitle: Vosotros vs Ustedes: Plural You in Spain vs Latin America
sections.content:
👥 PLURAL 'YOU' - Regional Differences

🇪🇸 SPAIN uses TWO forms:
• VOSOTROS/VOSOTRAS (informal plural)
• USTEDES (formal plural)

🌎 LATIN AMERICA uses ONE form:
• USTEDES (both formal and informal)

📍 VOSOTROS/AS (Spain only - informal):

Addressing multiple people informally (friends, family)

→ Vosotros habláis español
(You all speak Spanish - informal plural in Spain)

Conjugates with 2nd person plural: -áis, -éis, -ís
→ Vosotros tenéis (you all have)
→ Vosotros vivís (you all live)

📍 USTEDES (formal in Spain, all in Latin America):

Uses THIRD PERSON PLURAL conjugation (like ellos/ellas)
Even though it means 'you all'

→ Ustedes hablan español
(You all speak Spanish)

→ Ustedes tienen (you all have - 3rd person plural)

🇪🇸 IN SPAIN:
• Vosotros → friends/family
• Ustedes → strangers/formal

→ Vosotros sois mis amigos
(You are my friends - informal)

→ Ustedes son muy amables
(You are very kind - formal)

🌎 IN LATIN AMERICA:
• Only USTEDES used, regardless of formality

→ Ustedes son mis amigos
(You are my friends - using ustedes but informal situation)

⚠️ NO VOSOTROS in Latin America
Except in very formal writing or religious texts

💡 Know your target region when learning!

sections.subtitle: Formal Imperatives: Commands with Usted/Ustedes
sections.content:
📢 COMMANDS change form based on formality

👤 TÚ COMMANDS (informal):
• Affirmative = special forms (often 3rd person singular)
→ Habla (Speak!)
→ Come (Eat!)
→ Vive (Live!)

• Negative = present subjunctive
→ No hables (Don't speak!)
→ No comas (Don't eat!)

📋 USTED COMMANDS (formal):
Both affirmative AND negative use present subjunctive

→ Hable (usted) (Speak! - formal)
→ Coma (Eat! - formal)
→ Viva (Live! - formal)

→ No hable (Don't speak - formal)
→ No coma (Don't eat - formal)

👥 USTEDES COMMANDS (formal in Spain, all in Latin America):
Use present subjunctive plural

→ Hablen (ustedes) (Speak! - plural formal)
→ Coman (Eat! - plural)
→ No hablen (Don't speak - plural)

🇪🇸 VOSOTROS COMMANDS (informal plural, Spain only):
• Affirmative = infinitive with -d
→ Hablad (Speak! - you all)
→ Comed (Eat!)
→ Vivid (Live!)

• Negative = present subjunctive
→ No habléis (Don't speak! - vosotros)

💡 POLITENESS IN COMMANDS:
Add 'por favor' (please)

→ Hable más despacio, por favor
(Speak more slowly, please - formal)

📍 Common formal commands:
• Pase (Come in)
• Siéntese (Sit down)
• Dígame (Tell me / How can I help you?)
• Disculpe (Excuse me)

sections.subtitle: Politeness Strategies: Conditional & Subjunctive
sections.content:
🎯 POLITENESS STRATEGIES

Beyond tú/usted, use various strategies to sound polite

🔄 CONDITIONAL for polite requests:

Instead of direct statements, use conditional (less demanding)

Direct:
→ ¿Puedes ayudarme? (Can you help me? - informal)

Polite:
→ ¿Podrías ayudarme? (Could you help me? - softer)

→ ¿Querrías venir?
(Would you want to come? - more polite than quieres)

→ Me gustaría hablar contigo
(I would like to talk to you - softer than quiero)

💡 SUBJUNCTIVE with QUISIERA:

Imperfect subjunctive of querer = VERY polite

→ Quisiera un café, por favor
(I would like a coffee, please - very polite, more than quiero)

→ Quisiera hacer una pregunta
(I would like to ask a question - polite)

🔄 PODER (could/can):

'Podría' (conditional) more polite than 'puede'

→ ¿Podría ayudarme?
(Could you help me? - formal, very polite)

💬 INDIRECT QUESTIONS (more polite):

→ Me pregunto si podrías...
(I wonder if you could...)

→ ¿Te importaría...?
(Would you mind...?)

📍 PERMISSION:

→ ¿Podría pasar? (Could I come in? - polite)
→ ¿Le importa si...? (Do you mind if...? - formal)

🌸 DIMINUTIVES for politeness:

→ Un momentito (just a little moment - softer)
→ Un cafecito (a little coffee - friendlier)

💡 EXPRESSIONS:
• Si no es molestia (if it's not a bother)
• Cuando puedas (whenever you can)
• Si fuera/fuese posible (if it were possible)

sections.subtitle: More Politeness: Expressions & Avoiding Directness
sections.content:
🎯 AVOIDING DIRECT STATEMENTS

Spanish values indirect communication in polite contexts

💭 Instead of direct negatives, use softeners:

Direct:
→ No puedo (I can't)

Softer:
→ Me temo que no puedo (I'm afraid I can't)
→ Lamentablemente no puedo (Unfortunately I can't)

💭 Instead of 'No', use 'Es que...':

→ Es que... (It's just that... - excuse/explanation)
→ Es que no tengo tiempo
(It's just that I don't have time - softer refusal)

🙏 APOLOGETIC:

→ Disculpe/Perdone (Excuse me/Pardon me - formal)
→ Perdona/Disculpa (Sorry - informal)
→ Siento molestar (I'm sorry to bother)
→ Perdone que le interrumpa (Pardon me for interrupting - formal)

📋 MAKING REQUESTS:

Frame as questions rather than commands

Instead of:
→ Dame el libro (Give me the book - direct)

Use:
→ ¿Me das el libro? (Will you give me the book?)
→ ¿Me darías el libro? (Would you give me? - conditional)
→ ¿Podrías darme el libro? (Could you give me? - very polite)

✅ RESPONDING POLITELY:

To thanks:
• De nada (You're welcome)
• No hay de qué (Don't mention it)
• Con mucho gusto (With pleasure)

To requests:
• Con mucho gusto (With pleasure)
• Por supuesto (Of course)
• Cómo no (Of course/Why not - Latin America)

❌ DECLINING POLITELY:

→ Muchas gracias, pero...
(Thank you very much, but...)

→ Te lo agradezco, pero...
(I appreciate it, but...)

💡 These strategies show cultural competence beyond just grammar

sections.subtitle: Register-Appropriate Vocabulary & Situations
sections.content:
📊 REGISTER (language formality level)

Appropriate for different situations

💬 INFORMAL REGISTER (friends, family):

• Use tú, vosotros (in Spain)
• Colloquial vocabulary, contractions, slang
• Can omit subject pronouns, use incomplete sentences

Common slang:
→ Tío/Tía (dude - Spain slang)
→ Vale (OK - Spain)
→ ¿Qué onda? (What's up? - Mexico)
→ Chévere (Cool - Latin America)

📋 NEUTRAL REGISTER (everyday interactions):

• Clear, standard Spanish
• Use usted with strangers initially
• Correct grammar, everyday vocabulary
• In stores, restaurants, with acquaintances

→ Buenos días, ¿cómo está?
(Good morning, how are you? - neutral/formal)

👔 FORMAL REGISTER (professional, academic, official):

• Always usted/ustedes
• Complete sentences, precise vocabulary
• Subjunctive used correctly, no slang

→ Me gustaría solicitar información
(I would like to request information - formal)

→ Le agradezco su atención
(I thank you for your attention - formal)

Business emails:
→ Estimado/a señor/a (Dear Sir/Madam)
→ Atentamente (Sincerely)

📚 ACADEMIC:

• Passive voice more common
• Complex structures

→ Se llevó a cabo un estudio
(A study was carried out - formal/academic)

📖 VERY FORMAL/LITERARY:

→ Vuestra merced (Your grace - archaic, origin of usted)

Religious: Vos forms in liturgy

🌍 REGIONAL VARIATIONS:

Vocabulary choices signal register and region:
→ Coche (car - Spain) vs Carro/Auto (Latin America)

💡 Choose appropriate register for context
Using too informal in formal situations shows lack of cultural awareness

questions.question: When do you use TÚ?

answers.text: With friends, family, children, peers (informal contexts)

questions.hint: TÚ = informal. Use with friends, family, peers in casual situations.

questions.question: When do you use USTED?

answers.text: With strangers, elders, authority figures, professional contexts

questions.hint: USTED = formal. Use to show respect with strangers, elders, professionals.

questions.question: 'Tú hablas' vs 'Usted habla' - Why different verb forms?

answers.text: Usted uses third person conjugation even though it means 'you'

questions.hint: Key rule: USTED conjugates like él/ella (third person), not like tú (second person).

questions.question: 'Tú tienes' formally becomes...
questions.hint: USTED uses third person: tiene (like él/ella tiene), not tienes.

questions.question: In doubt, which form should you start with?

answers.text: USTED (formal) - wait for cues to switch to tú

questions.hint: When uncertain, start formal (USTED) and wait for the other person to suggest tú.

questions.question: Which form is used in SPAIN for informal plural 'you'?
questions.hint: Spain uses VOSOTROS for informal plural you (you all - friends/family).

questions.question: Which form is used in LATIN AMERICA for plural 'you' (all contexts)?
questions.hint: Latin America ONLY uses USTEDES for plural you (formal and informal contexts).

questions.question: 'Vosotros habláis' vs 'Ustedes hablan' - What's the pattern?

answers.text: Vosotros = 2nd person plural; Ustedes = 3rd person plural conjugation

questions.hint: VOSOTROS = 2nd person plural (habláis). USTEDES = 3rd person plural (hablan, like ellos).

questions.question: Is VOSOTROS used in Mexico?

answers.text: No - Latin America only uses ustedes

questions.hint: VOSOTROS is Spain only. Latin America (including Mexico) uses USTEDES for all plural you.

questions.question: Formal command (usted): 'Hablar' (to speak) becomes...
questions.hint: USTED commands use present subjunctive: Hable (usted) = Speak! (formal).

questions.question: Formal negative command: 'Don't speak' (usted) is...
questions.hint: Formal commands (affirmative and negative) use subjunctive: No hable.

questions.question: Informal affirmative command (tú): 'Come' means...
questions.hint: Come = Eat! (informal tú command). Context determines if command or indicative.

questions.question: Common formal command meaning 'Come in':
questions.hint: PASE (usted) = Come in! (formal). Very common in shops, offices.

questions.question: '¿Puedes ayudarme?' vs '¿Podrías ayudarme?' - Which is more polite?
questions.hint: CONDITIONAL (podrías = could you?) is more polite than present (puedes = can you?).

questions.question: 'Quisiera un café' - What does quisiera express?
questions.hint: QUISIERA (imperfect subjunctive of querer) = I would like (very polite, softer than quiero).

questions.question: '¿Podría ayudarme?' vs '¿Puede ayudarme?' - Which is more polite?
questions.hint: PODRÍA (conditional) = could you? More polite/softer than PUEDE (can you?).

questions.question: 'Me temo que no puedo' vs 'No puedo' - Which is more polite?

answers.text: Me temo que no puedo (I'm afraid I can't - softer)

questions.hint: Softeners like 'Me temo que' (I'm afraid that) make refusals more polite and indirect.

questions.question: 'Es que no tengo tiempo' - What does 'Es que' do?

answers.text: Makes it more direct and forceful

questions.hint: ES QUE = It's just that... (softener for excuses/refusals, less direct than blunt 'no').

questions.question: Instead of 'Dame el libro' (Give me the book), more polite is...

answers.text: ¿Podrías darme el libro? (Could you give me...?)
Dame el libro ahora (Give me the book now)

questions.hint: Frame as polite question with conditional: ¿Podrías...? (Could you...?) instead of direct command.

questions.question: Response to 'Gracias' (Thank you):

answers.text: De nada / No hay de qué (You're welcome / Don't mention it)

questions.hint: DE NADA or NO HAY DE QUÉ = You're welcome (standard responses to thanks).

questions.question: Which is INFORMAL register vocabulary?

answers.text: Me gustaría solicitar (I would like to request)

questions.hint: Informal register uses slang and colloquialisms: Tío, Vale, ¿Qué onda?, Chévere.

questions.question: Which is FORMAL register for business email?
questions.hint: Formal email: Estimado/a (Dear), Atentamente (Sincerely), Le agradezco (I thank you).

questions.question: What does appropriate REGISTER mean?

answers.text: Matching formality level to the situation/context
Always using the most formal Spanish
Always using slang to sound natural

questions.hint: REGISTER = formality level appropriate for context. Informal with friends, formal at work, neutral in shops.

questions.question: 'Disculpe' vs 'Disculpa' - What's the difference?

answers.text: Disculpe is formal (usted); Disculpa is informal (tú)
Disculpe is plural; Disculpa is singular
Both are exactly the same formality

questions.hint: DISCULPE (usted command) = Excuse me (formal). DISCULPA (tú command) = Excuse me (informal).
